lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first unguarded declaration of love sets the whole correspondence in motion.

lines.text: Is it indeed true that I was so near to the pleasure and honour of making your acquaintance? and can it be true that you look back upon the lost opportunity with any regret?
lines.note: Elizabeth answers Robert's hint that he had almost seen her.

lines.text: Who told you of my sculls and spider webs--Horne?
lines.note: Robert's skulls and spider webs become a running private joke.

lines.text: Who told me of your skulls and spiders?
lines.note: Elizabeth claims she knew Robert's skulls without being told.

lines.text: Next Wednesday--if you know how happy you make me! may I not say that, my dear friend, when I feel it from my soul?
lines.note: Robert counts down to another visit and the joy it brings.

lines.text: So, till to-morrow,--my light through the dark week.
lines.note: Robert calls Elizabeth his light through the dark week.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: Robert wraps his whole life around Elizabeth in a love letter.

lines.text: It comes at eight o'clock--the post says eight ...
lines.note: Elizabeth greets the postman's knock as the arrival of Robert's letter.

lines.text: My love--no words could serve here, but there is life before us, and to the end of it the vibration now struck will extend--I will live and die with your beautiful ring, your beloved hair--comforting me, blessing me.
lines.note: Robert pledges to live and die with Elizabeth's ring and hair.

lines.text: So I put the hair into his locket, which I wear habitually, and which never had hair before--the natural use of it being for perfume:--and this is the best perfume for all hours, besides the completing of a prophecy.
lines.note: Elizabeth keeps Robert's hair in a locket and completes a prophecy.

lines.text: Ah, the chestnut tree: do you think that I never saw the chestnut tree before?
lines.note: Elizabeth recalls Robert's chestnut tree and west wind from an early letter.

lines.text: Do you remember when you wrote first to me ‘May God bless you and me in that!’
lines.note: Elizabeth remembers Robert's first blessing before they met.

lines.text: Beside I got tired with the long walk from Carlyle’s last night—for I went and saw him to heart’s content—and he talked characteristically and well, and constringingly, bracingly.
lines.note: Robert returns from Carlyle with news and affection.

lines.text: Now let me kiss you—which kiss, as I am to really kiss you to-morrow, my sweetest, I shall dare tell the truth of to myself, and say ‘The real will be better.’
lines.note: Robert kisses Elizabeth in anticipation of seeing her next day.
